headline: New moon springs load the rivers — stripers stack the sunset flood as mackerel run thick off Monhegan
subhead: Big water this weekend puts bass in the river mouths at dusk, while cod and haddock hold deep in the Bay against a cold upwelling push.
body_markdown:
Last week the wind sat out of the northeast more mornings than not, and that's the kind of wind that does something specific to this coast — it shoves the warm skin water offshore and lets colder bottom water well up underneath it. You could feel it stepping off the boat at Eastern Egg Rock and at the Monhegan mooring field — the air had that raw edge to it even with the sun out, and the surface felt a good clip cooler than it did two weeks back. That upwelling has kept the groundfish honest. Cod, haddock, and pollock in Penobscot Bay have stayed down in the cooler water instead of creeping up onto the shallower humps like they will in a warm stretch, and that's actually been good news for anybody willing to fish deep and patient.

We're coming into new moon now, peaking through the weekend, and that means spring tides — the biggest exchange we'll see until the next cycle. Fox Islands Thorofare and Eggemoggin Reach are going to be hauling water hard on both the flood and the drain, and out at Monhegan the current off White Head and the backside ledges is going to rip through midtide like a river. That kind of flow pushes bait — herring, mackerel, peanut bunker — and it pushes it hard, which is exactly why the sunset flood at the river mouths has turned into the thing to chase this week. Big springs concentrate feed in the funnel points, and predators know it. St. George River mouth, the Medomak, the run at Damariscotta — all of them are worth a look on that last two hours of incoming water right up through dusk.

Striper action has been real but not a gimme. I had three trips out toward the mouth of the St. George in the last ten days, connected on two of them, and the pattern was consistent — nothing doing on the early flood, then the fish showed up hard in that last hour and a half before and right at sunset, right as the current really got moving on this building spring tide. Schoolies mostly, 22 to 28 inches, with a few better fish mixed in that felt like keeper-class when they leaned into the drag. Swimming a white or bone Redfin along the current seams where the fresh water meets the salt has been the most consistent producer, and a chunk of mackerel on a fish-finder rig, drifted right through the funnel on the last of the incoming, has taken a couple of the bigger fish. If you fish it, get there before the tide peaks — once it goes to high stand and starts to slack, the bite shuts off almost like someone flipped a switch.

Mackerel have been thick around Eastern Egg Rock and off the east side of Monhegan, schools stacked from the surface down to about 35 feet over structure. Standard mackerel trees with a bit of bright jig on the bottom hook have been filling coolers fast on a slow bite window — you can tell when they're there because the birds are working the same water, terns diving and the puffins cutting through. That's also brought a few bluefish into the mix around Egg Rock, chopping bait on top in the early morning calm before the wind builds. Nothing giant — cocktail blues mostly — but they'll hit a small metal jig or a Deadly Dick worked fast on the surface, and it's a nice change of pace between mackerel drops.

Groundfish in the Bay have been the tougher story, and I'll be straight about it — this cold upwelled water has the cod and haddock down deep and a little sluggish, not aggressive the way they get when the thermocline sets up just right. Best luck has come from the channel between Vinalhaven and North Haven and out toward the deeper water off Matinicus, working diamond jigs and bar rigs tipped with clam belly down in 120 to 150 feet, right on bottom, slow lift-and-drop with long pauses. Pollock have actually been the more reliable eating fish this week — schooling up over the humps in 60 to 90 feet around the Fox Islands and hitting jigs worked with a bit more speed higher in the water column, 30 to 50 feet down. If you want fish for the table with less patience required, that's where I'd point the bow.

Looking ahead, this new moon spring tide peaks right through Monday, and that's the window I'd fish hardest for stripers at the river mouths — the flood-to-sunset overlap is about as good an alignment as you get up here, current, light, and bait all lining up together. If the wind backs off the northeast and lets the surface warm back up even a couple degrees, I'd expect the cod and haddock to come up a bit shallower and turn more aggressive, so that's worth checking again toward the end of the week. Mackerel should hold at Egg Rock and Monhegan for now, though once these big tides start really flushing bait out of the bay, they have a habit of pushing farther offshore fast — if you want a box of mackerel for bait or the table, I wouldn't wait too long. Plan A this week is the sunset flood at the river mouths; Plan B, if the bass don't show or the wind kicks up onshore and muddies the funnel, is running out to the mackerel schools and picking off a bluefish or two while you're at it. Either way, respect the current on these springs — it's moving a lot of water fast, and that cuts both ways for the fish and for you.
